opus-5.5.text:
I think they're almost two different problems, even if the underlying models look similar.

With conversational audio, the dominant constraint is latency. When you talk to someone, you expect a response within a few hundred milliseconds. If the system takes two seconds, the interaction feels broken, even if what it says is perfect. So you're forced into streaming architectures. You have to start generating before you've fully "decided" what you're going to say, and you have to handle interruptions, overlapping speech, backchannels like "mm-hm," and turn-taking. A lot of that is about timing and responsiveness rather than raw quality. Small artifacts in the voice are forgiven if the conversation feels natural and alive.

A standalone artifact, like a narrated video, a podcast segment, or a piece of music with visuals, is the opposite. Nobody cares if it took thirty seconds or five minutes to produce. What matters is that the final output holds up to repeated, careful listening. People will notice a slightly wrong intonation, a lip-sync drift of a few frames, or a voice that subtly changes timbre halfway through. So you can afford non-causal models, multiple passes, looking ahead and revising, and generally spending much more compute per second of output to get consistency and polish.

There's also a difference in what "correct" means. In conversation, the content has to be grounded in what the other person just said, so the reasoning and understanding side matters enormously. The audio is a vehicle for an exchange. In a produced artifact, the audio *is* the product, so aesthetics, coherence over long durations, and control, letting a creator say "make this part slower, more emotional," become much more important.

So in practice you end up optimizing very different trade-offs: speed, robustness, and interactivity on one side, versus fidelity, long-range consistency, and controllability on the other. Long term, I think the interesting challenge is getting models good enough that you don't have to choose as much, but today those are still quite distinct engineering targets.

r001.rationale: It says conversational audio is dominated by latency and expects a reply within a few hundred milliseconds.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the low-latency requirement forces streaming architectures.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, because the two look similar on the surface, they're both "audio from a model," but the constraints are almost opposite.

With a standalone artifact, say you're generating a short video with a voiceover, or a music clip, the model gets to think as long as it wants. You can run a big diffusion model, you can do many sampling steps, you can even generate several candidates and pick the best one. Latency is basically irrelevant. What matters is quality at the end, and coherence across the whole thing. The user hits a button and waits ten seconds, thirty seconds, it's fine.

Conversation is the opposite. The thing that matters most is not peak quality, it's the latency and the fact that you can't stop. If I'm talking to you and you take two seconds before answering, it feels broken. Humans respond in something like two hundred milliseconds, sometimes they start talking before you've even finished. So the model has to be streaming, both on the input side and the output side. It has to listen while it speaks. That's a full-duplex problem, and it changes the architecture completely. You can't have the classic pipeline of speech recognition, then an LLM, then text-to-speech, because each stage adds delay and you lose everything that isn't text, the tone, the hesitations, the interruptions.

The other thing is that in conversation, errors are cheap but they are permanent. You cannot go back and resample a sentence you already said out loud. So you need a model that is robust in a kind of monotone way, it should be good enough on every single frame, rather than brilliant on average with occasional disasters. For an artifact you'd rather have the opposite, high variance is fine if you can select afterward.

And then there's the question of what the model is optimizing for. An artifact is optimized to be consumed, so you want it dense, polished. In a dialogue, you actually want the model to say less, to leave room, to handle being interrupted gracefully. A lot of the work is not in generating speech, it's in deciding when not to.

So from the modeling side, when we worked on this, the key ideas were to operate directly on audio tokens at a fixed frame rate, keep the model causal, and have it model both streams, the user and itself, jointly. Once you do that, a lot of things that look like hard engineering problems, like turn-taking, become things the model just learns from data.

r001.rationale: The response says latency matters most in conversation and that a two-second delay feels broken.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the model has to be streaming on both input and output, presenting streaming as a central requirement.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is latency. If you’re generating a standalone video with audio, you can take some time to produce it, and you can optimize for the quality of the final result. The user is going to watch it once it’s ready.

In a conversation, the timing is part of the quality. If I ask you a question and you wait five seconds before answering, even a very good answer feels unnatural. You need to start responding quickly, generate the audio as you go, and handle interruptions. If I start speaking while you’re answering, you need to adapt rather than just finish playing something you already generated.

So it’s not just about making a voice sound realistic. It’s about making the whole interaction feel natural—the pauses, the turn-taking, and how quickly the system reacts.

r001.rationale: It says latency is the main difference and that waiting five seconds feels unnatural, so conversational audio needs to respond very quickly.

r002.rationale: It describes starting quickly and generating audio as it goes, which communicates streaming as a central design consideration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difference is latency. If you’re generating a standalone video, you can spend some time producing it, and the person watches it when it’s ready. In a conversation, the time it takes to respond is part of the experience. You can have very good audio quality, but if the system takes several seconds to answer every time, it’s going to feel very unnatural.

You also need to handle interruptions and understand when someone has finished speaking. People hesitate, pause, or start talking while the other person is still speaking. So it’s not just about generating a good audio sample. It’s about making the whole interaction work in real time.

r001.rationale: It says latency is the main difference and that taking several seconds to respond feels unnatural, emphasizing the need for very fast conversational responses.

r002.rationale: It discusses real-time interaction and interruptions, but does not identify streaming as a design consideration.
